Jérôme Souchier (1508–1571) was a French Roman Catholic cardinal. He was born in Auvergne, France, and died in 1571. Souchier was created cardinal by Pope Pius IV in 1556, following a series of diplomatic maneuvers that ultimately led to his appointment. As cardinal, he played a key role in the Council of Trent, a major ecumenical council that aimed to reform the Catholic Church. The council, which took place from 1545 to 1563, was a significant event in the history of the Church, as it marked a turning point in the reform of Catholic doctrine and practices. Souchier's involvement in the council reflects his influential position within the Church and his commitment to its reform. His legacy as a cardinal continues to be felt in the history of the Catholic Church, particularly in the context of the Council of Trent. The council's decrees, which were largely drafted by Souchier and other cardinals, remain a cornerstone of Catholic theology to this day.

Souchier's life and career were marked by a series of diplomatic appointments and promotions, which ultimately led to his elevation to the cardinalate. In 1551, he was appointed as the Bishop of Noyon, a position that gave him significant influence within the Church. This appointment was followed by his appointment as the Bishop of Beauvais in 1556, a position that further solidified his position within the Church.

Souchier's legacy extends beyond his role as a cardinal, as he played a key role in shaping the course of Catholic history. His involvement in the Council of Trent, which took place from 1545 to 1563, was a significant event in the history of the Church, as it marked a turning point in the reform of Catholic doctrine and practices.
